title: Captives freed from Nadir Shah
hook: in 1739 Sikh horsemen raided the retreating Persian army and freed captives

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh, a father and son in Lahore who would not give way. Your line was father and son. Who did you reach out to? Day eight hundred fifty-six.

A long column moves along the road out of India. Camels and carts loaded with treasure. Soldiers. And among them, on foot, roped together, people who did not choose to be there: men and women taken from the cities the army had plundered, being marched toward a foreign country they would likely never leave. This was the army of Nadir Shah, the ruler of Persia, going home. Nobody, it seemed, could stop it. Then, at night, horsemen began to appear at the edges of the column. Today: captives freed from Nadir Shah.
screen: `A COLUMN OF TREASURE AND CAPTIVES.` → `NADIR SHAH GOES HOME.` → `HORSEMEN AT THE EDGES, AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Nadir Shah had invaded from Persia and sacked Delhi. Tradition says his army left carrying not only treasure but captives. As it crossed the Punjab on the way back, it passed through the forests and river country where the Khalsa had been living on horseback. These were the riders this path met in the forests: hunted, scattered, with a price on their heads. They had every reason to stay out of the way of a conqueror's army. Instead, tradition says, the jathas struck the rear of the column again and again, in quick night raids. They took back some of the plunder. And they cut loose the captives. The Sikhs did not keep the freed people as prizes, or leave them by the road. Tradition says they escorted them back toward their homes and families. People who had been dragged away found themselves, a few days later, being walked home by strangers on horseback. Nadir Shah, it's said, asked the governor of Lahore who these raiders were. He was told they were Sikhs, that they had no homes but their saddles, and that they could not be caught. Nadir Shah is said to have replied that such people would one day rule the land. Whether he said it or not, Sikhs remember the exchange. The deeper thread is older than Nadir Shah. Sikhs call Guru Hargobind Bandi Chhor, the one who freed captives. In these years his Sikhs did the same, on horseback, at night.
screen: `AN ARMY GOING HOME WITH CAPTIVES.` · `NIGHT RAIDS ON THE REAR.` · `THE FREED ARE WALKED HOME.` · `NO HOMES BUT THEIR SADDLES.` · then, large: `CAPTIVES BROUGHT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone get home. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who is far from home right now, in any sense. A student a long way from family. A neighbor new to the country. Someone stuck in a hospital, a job or a situation they can't easily leave. A friend who has lost their way back to themselves. Picture one small thing that would bring them a step closer. A ride. A meal that tastes like home. A phone call. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bandi Chhor, freer of captives. The name Sikhs give Guru Hargobind, echoed when his Sikhs cut loose the prisoners of a retreating Persian army and, tradition says, walked them home. Today's word.
Your line: captives brought home. Today, do one concrete thing to help someone get home, or feel a little closer to it. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs retell the freeing of Nadir Shah's captives as part of the Khalsa's history of protecting the defenseless, and remember Guru Hargobind as Bandi Chhor, the freer of captives, at Bandi Chhor Divas.
